items.title: Theologian Uncovers Dangerous ‘Common Sense’ Hidden in Kids’ Movies Today
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Parents, beware.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Very often, the truth is hiding in plain sight. That’s certainly the case with much of children’s entertainment.

The underlying message affixed to any number of movies geared toward kids seems to be some version of following one’s own heart, listening to his desires, chasing after her feelings. But that message, according to Trevin Wax, is a direct contradiction to the Gospel.

Wax, an author and visiting professor at Cedarville University, recently appeared on CBN’s “Faith in Culture,” were he eschewed such ideologies. While the world calls those ideas “common sense,” he said they are incongruous with Christianity.

“You think of these slogans that are out there, like, ‘Be true to yourself,’ ‘You do you,’ ‘Live your truth,’ ‘You are enough,’ ‘Follow your heart,’ ‘Chase your dreams,'” he said. “Sociologists call that ‘expressive individualism.’ … That’s the plot line in so many movies, even, like, good wholesome movies, in Disney movies. … It kind of passes for common sense in our day and age.”

The secular understanding of “freedom” is a far cry from true freedom as explained in Scripture, Wax said.

“It’s just so easy to define freedom in our day as a freedom from constraints, from limitations,” he explained. “[The world says] freedom is me doing whatever I want to do, when the Bible actually teaches that, ‘No, you doing just whatever you want to do, especially in our flesh, is a kind of slavery.'”

Throughout the New Testament, the Apostle Paul explains human beings will always be slaves to something — either to sin and our own desires or to a just and merciful God whose ways are higher and better than our own.

In Romans 6:16, Paul wrote, “Don’t you realize that you become the slave of whatever you choose to obey? You can be a slave to sin, which leads to death, or you can choose to obey God, which leads to righteous living” (NLT).

“True freedom is submission to God, and it’s freedom for something,” said Wax. “[I]t’s not doing whatever we want; it’s aligning our wants with God’s will, recognizing that that’s when we’re truly freest.”

Wax is the author of the new book, “The Gospel Way Catechism for Kids,” a children’s edition of his book by the same title.

In it, he and his co-author, Thomas West, outline 50 faith-centered questions and answers for children to read, study, and talk about with their families. He explained that these catechisms should serve as conversation starters in the home.

“A catechism isn’t supposed to be everything,” he said. “It’s supposed to be something. It’s meant to give you the structure or the scaffolding that you can then come in later and begin to fill in.”

While the world teaches a “meditation” that empties the mind of everything, Wax emphasized a godly mindfulness that calls believers to fill their minds with the commands and promises of Scripture.

“We’ve got to distinguish the Christian understanding of prayer from just mindfulness routines or just Eastern meditation that leads us to sort of empty our minds,” he explained. “[B]iblical meditation … is a filling of the mind with Scripture and God’s Word.”

Catch our full conversation with Trevin Wax in the “Faith in Culture” episode above.

items.title: ‘Totally Demonic’: Jonathan Cahn Reveals What Really Happened With the Viral Duct-Taped Man on Plane
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Celebrated author and Messianic rabbi Jonathan Cahn is making headlines after revealing that he was the unnamed passenger who drew the ire of an allegedly irate man who was so out of control he needed to be duct taped to an airplane seat.

Cahn shared his account of the disturbing incident aboard American Airlines Flight 618, proclaiming that the widely circulated images of a passenger being duct-taped — and media accounts of what unfolded — did not tell the full story.

He told CBN News he was returning home after a number of interviews promoting his new book, “The Altar of Pergamon,” when his assigned seat was unexpectedly changed shortly before the flight. Little did he know that his new placement on the plane would yield an experience he’d never forget.

Cahn ended up sitting beside a man who he said initially appeared friendly. In fact, the two talked for roughly two hours, with the passenger asking about his books and discussing his own family — but then the situation shifted after Cahn prayed about whether God wanted him to share his faith with the man.

“I said, ‘Give me an opening to share salvation with him, and share love with him,’” he said.

According to Cahn, the conversation turned toward faith, and he shared his testimony of once being an atheist and eventually coming to believe in God. Then, he said, the man’s behavior abruptly changed.

“At that moment, I’ve never seen anything like this,” he said. “His face changes. His voice changes.”

Cahn described the transformation as dramatic and spiritual, saying, “It was like someone getting taken over.”

He said the passenger began cursing Jesus and God, making vulgar statements and disturbing other people aboard the aircraft. Cahn said the man later became friendly again before allegedly putting his hands around Cahn’s neck and lightly striking him.

One of the most unusual moments involved Cahn’s laptop. At one point, a black line appeared on his screen. He said the passenger then reached over and tapped the computer, forcing the black area to spread across the entire screen.

Cahn said the computer was particularly important because it contained his writings and other projects.

Then, the author felt God tell him to protect his computer because the devil would use the man to destroy it. Listening to this warning, he attempted to leave his seat with the laptop and alleged that this is when the passenger lunged for it.

“We are wrestling on the plane,” Cahn said, noting that the computer became the focal point of the chaos. “I mean, we are literally wrestling.”

Cahn said the pilot contacted the ground for an emergency landing as the confrontation continued. Eventually, two passengers, including a retired police officer, intervened. Flight attendants provided duct tape to restrain the man, and the plane landed in Baltimore, where authorities took the man into custody.

The irony of the entire incident is that Cohn’s latest book “The Altar of Pergamon” — which came out just before this incident — deals with themes surrounding the devil and spiritual warfare. He believes some of what unfolded on the flight is rooted in that spiritual battle.

“The warfare is real, the enemy is real, and God is real,” he said.

Despite what happened, Cahn said he has no desire to condemn the passenger. Instead, he said he prays for him, and he even delivered a message to him.

“God loves you,” he said. “God’s arms are open. He loves you and He’ll receive you and wash that all away and give you a new beginning.”

Watch the full interview for more on this shocking story.

items.title: Remember When Churches in the ’90s Had Sermons About Pokemon Being Demonic?
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Somewhere in your parents’ house there is probably a binder of Pokémon cards that got confiscated from you. There was a whole apparatus behind that: Special sermons. VHS tapes. At least one book. All of it arguing that Pikachu was the gateway to the occult. A clip from one of those tapes shows
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Somewhere in your parents’ house there is probably a binder of Pokémon cards that got confiscated from you.

There was a whole apparatus behind that: Special sermons. VHS tapes. At least one book. All of it arguing that Pikachu was the gateway to the occult.

A clip from one of those tapes shows a man in a dark suit holding up a Pokémon poster, explaining what the spiral on Poliwhirl’s belly really stands for.

Male fertility, he says. Also, the character used to be called Hypno, and they renamed it “to make it a little more innocent.”

Neither of those things is true. But he keeps going, and it gets better. Mewtwo holds up three fingers, and three fingers is not “hook ’em horns” and not “I love you” — “it means hail Satan.” Pikachu’s tail is “a satanic Z.” Pokémon cards come from Wizards of the Coast, and, he asks the room, what is a wizard? A male practitioner of black magic.

The speaker is Stephen Dollins, who toured the Prophecy Club circuit in the late ’90s billed as a former high priest in the Church of Satan. The sermon video runs 35 minutes.

He wasn’t the only one working this material. Around the same time, a Texas pastor named Phil Arms was telling his own congregation that Pokémon means pocket monster, that becoming a Pokémon master meant learning what New Age teaching says masters really do — “take control of spirits in the dark realm” — and that the whole thing was a game “that teaches children how to enter into the world of witchcraft.” In 2000 he published the book, which was called “Pokemon & Harry Potter: A Fatal Attraction.” At one point in his sermon he warns that there’s a devil and he hates your children. On screen, at that exact moment, is Jigglypuff.

For a stretch there, this was just the weather. Pokémon reached the U.S. in 1998, and within a year it was everywhere — lunchboxes, Burger King, a stack of cards in every kid’s back pocket. It landed in a church culture still running on the fumes of the Satanic Panic, the long moral scare over ritual abuse, backmasked records and Dungeons & Dragons. Jack Chick was still printing “Dark Dungeons,” the tract where a girl discovers her D&D group is a witch coven. The machinery was built and waiting. Pokémon walked right into it.

A post shared by RELEVANT Magazine (@relevantmagazine)

items.title: Psychotherapy or Confession?
items.author: Dr. D.P. Curtin
items.summary:
Dr. D.P. Curtin

In the Catholic world, it is more apparent—and it needs to be stated—that therapy and confession are not the same enterprise.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. D.P. Curtin

They say that everyone’s favorite subject is themselves. People are endlessly skilled in discussing themselves, their thoughts and feelings, their ideas for the way the world should be. Take any contemporary American and place them in a coffee shop, on a podcast, or in a therapist’s office, and they can produce a forty-five-minute dissertation on their childhood and all those assorted things that punctuate life. In the last quarter-century in particular, we have become connoisseurs of our own interiority. The language of psychology, once reserved for the consultation room, has puzzlingly entered into common usage. We know our attachment styles, our personality types, our love languages, our trauma responses, and perhaps even the unconscious motives that prevent us from finishing tasks. If self-knowledge alone could save us, ours would be the most pristine, most devout generation since the apostles walked in Galilee. However, perhaps self-knowledge alone is an incomplete discipline.

Something curious has happened in the wake of all this psychological banter. In short, the more fluent we have become in the language of psychological introspection—in the act of explaining ourselves—the less certain we seem about changing ourselves. This is by no means an indictment of psychotherapy or a claim against its efficaciousness. Good counseling has aided countless people from the personal trials of depression, addiction, anxiety, grief, and despair. It has given us the verbiage to rebuild communication and offered us recognition of our own need for boundaries and personal limitations. It would be foolish to deny the value of this in the face of overwhelming results.

However, there is some confusion relating to what psychotherapy is and what it can do. In the Catholic world, it is more apparent—and it needs to be stated—that therapy and confession are not the same enterprise. They are relatives, not twins. For the unfamiliar, there has been speculation that Freud got the idea for his “talking cure” in his own Viennese childhood. His Austrian Catholic nanny would often take him to church, and he would observe firsthand the affective changes that took place before and after the sacrament of auricular confession. Taking this account at face value, this would make confession something akin to psychotherapy’s great-grandfather. However, with this, as with most relations, there are considerably different qualities to both of these crafts. The first of which is an orientation to the subject. That is to say, psychotherapy ordinarily asks, What happened to you? while confession asks, What have you done? The difference here is not trivial, albeit subtle. One question seeks understanding. The other is seeking something alien to the realm of psychology: the idea of repentance.

Suffice it to say that modern people greatly prefer the first because it allows us to remain self‑preoccupied. Psychotherapy is built on the premise of constructivism, that you are the authority on your own life, happiness, and the pursuit of the good in the world. The second is considerably less flattering. It insists that after every generous allowance has been made for our upbringing, there still remains one stubborn fact: We are responsible for ourselves. We possess the free will capable of making the decisions that ultimately plague us. In the words of the late Edwin Arnold, “Ye suffer from yourselves, none else compels.”

To be frank, there is no market for that kind of observation. As a rule latent found across our civilization, human beings have always preferred complicated explanations to simple confessions. It is comforting and perhaps self-aggrandizing to imagine ourselves as elaborate machines requiring expert technical calibration. Every age invents new vocabularies for old vices, as though a change in terminology amounted to a change in human nature. It is rather less pleasant to admit the obvious fact that pride, vanity, and selfishness have survived through every century without requiring much in terms of innovation. The old hypocrites of yesteryear at least paid virtue the compliment of imitation.

The sacrament of confession is radical precisely because it refuses to let us be passive in our actions, to become spectators of our own moral lives. It does not permit the participant to be detached. It invites us to analyze our misgivings and personal failings from a safe academic distance. It requires us to stand inside the moral wreckage of our own actions and admit, without annotation or legal counsel, “I am the one accountable.” In the era that we live in, that sentence has become unambiguously countercultural. We are inhabitants of an age that is remarkably proficient at distributing blame—or rather finding absolution for ourselves and condemnation for others. Our vices are accompanied by a long personal genealogy of behavior. Every one of our failings has a context, and every one of our cruelties possesses a reasonable explanatory framework. While some of those explanations are in fact valid and deserve thoughtful consideration, explanation and absolution are very different things.

To explain why a bridge collapsed is not the same as rebuilding it. Likewise, understanding why we sin, why we have transgressed the natural moral order of the world, does not reconcile us with God or with our neighbor. It only provides the prologue, the route by which we brought ourselves there. The act of any confession begins where explanation ends.

The state of our culture has become emotionally allergic to any sense of judgment. For the lay person, the idea of judgment is akin to moral violence. Perversely, our culture has imagined freedom as the absence of any kind of judgment, and in doing so, has created a landscape of perpetual and inexhaustible nihilism. Christianity proposes something altogether stranger. Our freedom begins not with moral judgment but with truthful judgment. I help no one by condemning them, but I also cannot help them if I deny them the truth that they need. A person who cannot admit to their own sin, who is not responsible for themselves, is not liberated from sin but a slave to their own insanity.

The confessional performs a remarkable act, something which has little parallel in the course of Western civilization. It removes every respectable disguise we all carry. There is no room for temporal authority. There is no room for political opinion or professional accomplishments. In the end, there are no excuses. Inside, there is only the sinner asking for mercy. It is difficult to think of another institution in our civilization that so thoroughly levels any notion of human pride. The Church does not ask whether your failures were sophisticated or what unconscious forces drove you to act. It only asks whether they are yours and you repent of them.

If my deepest problem is only my environment, the society I live in, the friends or family that surround me, then I must wait for the whole rest of the world to improve before I can become better. Obviously, such a proposition is impossible, and it shifts accountability to everyone and anyone. If everything is determined by forces outside my control, then genuine moral transformation becomes exceedingly difficult to imagine. Christianity, with its proposition of sin, redemption, and renewal, proposes a harder diagnosis but a brighter hope.

Sin is real, but so is the presence of grace. The Christian leaves the confessional with something no amount of self-analysis can provide: not insight into the nebulous past but reconciliation for the future. Psychotherapy may help us understand why we fell and offer us the natural comfort of connecting with another human being. However, confession assures us that, by God’s grace, we need not remain on the ground. In an age devoted to explaining ourselves, that may be the most subversive idea of all.

Charlie Dyer’s devotional takes us back to Joshua. It’s all this week on The Land and the Book.
